items.t: Hypertension; stable chronic angina; stable chronic heart failure with reduced systolic left ventricular function (added to ACE inhibitor and diuretic, optionally cardiac glycoside).

src.q: Treatment of Hypertension Treatment of stable chronic angina Treatment of stable chronic heart failure with reduced systolic left ventricular function in addition to ACE inhibitors, and diuretics, and optionally cardiac glycosides

items.t: Another UK bisoprolol 5 mg SmPC lists only hypertension and angina pectoris.

src.q: 1. The management of hypertension. 2. The management of angina pectoris.

items.t: Heart failure: the treating physician should be experienced in managing chronic heart failure; patients must be stable (no acute failure) when starting.

src.q: It is recommended that the treating physician should be experienced in the management of chronic heart failure.
Patients should be stable (without acute failure) when bisoprolol treatment is initiated.

items.t: Adults: start 5 mg once daily; usual dose 10 mg once daily; maximum 20 mg per day.

src.q: It is recommended to start with 5 mg per day. The usual dose is 10mg once daily, with a maximum recommended dose of 20mg per day.

items.t: Stable chronic heart failure: titrate 1.25 mg once daily for 1 week, then 2.5 mg, 3.75 mg (1 week each), 5 mg and 7.5 mg (4 weeks each), then 10 mg once daily maintenance; maximum 10 mg once daily. Monitor heart rate, blood pressure and heart failure symptoms during titration.

src.q: 1.25 mg once daily for 1 week, if well tolerated increase to 2.5 mg once daily for a further week
increase to 10 mg once daily for the maintenance therapy The maximum recommended dose is 10 mg once daily.
Close monitoring of vital signs (heart rate, blood pressure) and symptoms of worsening heart failure is recommended during the titration phase.

items.t: Stopping: do not stop suddenly; reduce slowly by halving the dose weekly.

src.q: The dose should be diminished slowly by weekly halving of the dose.

items.t: Elderly: no dose adjustment normally needed.

src.q: Elderly No dosage adjustment is normally required.

items.t: No paediatric experience; use cannot be recommended for children.

src.q: There is no paediatric experience with bisoprolol, therefore its use cannot be recommended for children.

items.t: Contraindicated (UK bisoprolol 5 mg SmPC, all patients): acute heart failure or decompensation needing IV inotropes; cardiogenic shock; sinoatrial block; second- or third-degree AV block (without pacemaker); symptomatic bradycardia (heart rate below 60 beats/min before starting); severe bronchial asthma or severe COPD; sick sinus syndrome; symptomatic hypotension (systolic blood pressure below 100 mmHg); severe peripheral arterial occlusive disease and Raynaud's syndrome; untreated phaeochromocytoma; metabolic acidosis; hypersensitivity to bisoprolol or excipients.

src.q: Bisoprolol is contraindicated in patients with:
acute heart failure or during episodes of heart failure decompensation requiring i.v. inotropic therapy
second or third degree AV block (without pacemaker).
symptomatic bradycardia (heart rate less than 60 beats/min prior to start of therapy).
severe bronchial asthma or severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
symptomatic hypotension (systolic blood pressure <100mmHg).
severe forms of peripheral arterial occlusive disease and Raynaud's syndrome.
untreated phaeochromocytoma (see section 4.4).
metabolic acidosis.
hypersensitivity to the active substance(s) or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1

items.t: Two other UK bisoprolol 5 mg SmPCs word the same 4.3 list as applying to chronic heart failure patients ("contraindicated in chronic heart failure patients with"); one of them names severe bronchial asthma only (no COPD). The list is kept as general contraindications because another UK bisoprolol SmPC states it for all patients.

Bisoprolol is contraindicated in chronic heart failure patients with acute heart failure

src.q: Especially in patients with ischemic heart disease the cessation of therapy with bisoprolol must not be done abruptly

items.t: Use with caution in: bronchospasm (asthma, obstructive airways disease; give bronchodilator; beta2-agonist dose may need increasing); diabetes with large glucose fluctuations (hypoglycaemia masked; severe hypoglycaemia risk with sulfonylureas); strict fasting; desensitisation therapy; first-degree AV block; Prinzmetal's angina; peripheral arterial occlusive disease; general anaesthesia.

items.t: Obstructive airways disease: another UK bisoprolol SmPC says avoid unless there are compelling clinical reasons; if used, start at the lowest dose and monitor for dyspnoea, exercise intolerance or cough.

src.q: these should be avoided in patients with obstructive airways diseases, unless there are compelling clinical reasons for their use.
Where such reasons exist, Bisoprolol may be used with caution.
the treatment with bisoprolol should be started at the lowest possible dose and patients should be carefully monitored for new symptoms (e.g. dyspnoea, exercise intolerance, cough).

items.t: Hypertension or angina with heart failure: use with caution.

src.q: Bisoprolol must be used with caution in patients with hypertension or angina pectoris and accompanying heart failure.

items.t: Psoriasis (or history): only after carefully balancing benefits against risks.

src.q: Patients with psoriasis or with a history of psoriasis should only be given beta-blockers (e.g. bisoprolol) after carefully balancing the benefits against the risks.

items.t: Allergy: may increase sensitivity to allergens and severity of anaphylaxis; adrenaline may not work as expected.

src.q: bisoprolol may increase both the sensitivity towards allergens and the severity of anaphylactic reactions. Adrenaline treatment does not always yield the expected therapeutic effect.

items.t: Phaeochromocytoma: give only after alpha-blockade. May mask thyrotoxicosis.

src.q: In patients with phaeochromocytoma bisoprolol must not be administered until after alpha-receptor blockade.
Under treatment with bisoprolol the symptoms of a thyreotoxicosis may be masked.

items.t: Surgery: continue beta-blockade peri-operatively; inform the anaesthetist. If withdrawal is needed, do it gradually and complete about 48 hours before anaesthesia.

src.q: It is currently recommended that maintenance beta-blockade be continued peri-operatively.
If it is thought necessary to withdraw beta-blocker therapy before surgery, this should be done gradually and completed about 48 hours before anaesthesia.

items.t: Heart failure: no experience in type 1 diabetes, severe renal or hepatic impairment, restrictive cardiomyopathy, congenital heart disease, significant valve disease, or MI within 3 months.

src.q: There is no therapeutic experience of bisoprolol treatment of heart failure in patients with the following diseases and conditions:

items.t: Verapamil (and, less so, diltiazem): not recommended; negative effect on contractility and AV conduction. IV verapamil in a patient on a beta-blocker may cause profound hypotension and AV block.

src.q: Calcium antagonists of the verapamil type and to a lesser extent of the diltiazem type: Negative influence on contractility and atrio-ventricular conduction.
Intravenous administration of verapamil in patients on β-blocker treatment may lead to profound hypotension and atrioventricular block.

items.t: Centrally acting antihypertensives (e.g. clonidine, methyldopa, moxonidine): not recommended; may worsen heart failure; abrupt withdrawal may cause rebound hypertension.

src.q: Centrally acting antihypertensive drugs such as clonidine and others (e.g. methyldopa, moxonodine, rilmenidine)
Abrupt withdrawal, particularly if prior to beta-blocker discontinuation, may increase risk of "rebound hypertension".

items.t: Dihydropyridines (e.g. amlodipine): use with caution; more risk of hypotension and possible further worsening of heart failure.

src.q: Calcium antagonists of the dihydropyridine type such as felodipine and amlodipine: Concomitant use may increase the risk of hypotension

items.t: Insulin and oral antidiabetics: increased glucose lowering; hypoglycaemia symptoms may be masked; sulfonylureas may increase the risk of severe hypoglycaemia.

src.q: Insulin and oral antidiabetic drugs: Increase of blood sugar lowering effect.
The concomitant use of beta-blockers with sulfonylureas could increase the risk of severe hypoglycaemia

items.t: NSAIDs may reduce the blood pressure lowering effect. Antihypertensives and other blood pressure lowering medicines (e.g. tricyclic antidepressants) may increase the risk of hypotension.

src.q: NSAIDs may reduce the hypotensive effect of bisoprolol.

Concomitant use with antihypertensive agents as well as with other drugs with blood pressure lowering potential (e.g. tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates, phenothiazines) may increase the risk of hypotension.

items.t: Sympathomimetics: beta-agonists (e.g. isoprenaline) may lose effect; alpha- and beta-agonists (e.g. adrenaline) may raise blood pressure.

src.q: Sympathomimetics that activate both β- and α-adrenoceptors (e.g. noradrenaline, adrenaline): Combination with bisoprolol may unmask the α-adrenoceptor-mediated vasoconstrictor effects

items.t: MAOIs (except MAO-B inhibitors): enhanced hypotensive effect but also risk of hypertensive crisis. Digoxin and parasympathomimetics: more bradycardia/AV delay. Class I and III antiarrhythmics: AV conduction effects. Mefloquine: more bradycardia.

src.q: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (except MAO-B inhibitors): Enhanced hypotensive effect of the beta-blockers but also risk for hypertensive crisis.
Digitalis glycosides: Reduction of heart rate, increase of atrio-ventricular conduction time.

items.t: Severe renal impairment (CrCl below 20 ml/minute): do not exceed 10 mg once daily (hypertension/angina).

src.q: In patients with severe renal impairment (creatinine clearance <20ml/minute), the dose should not exceed 10mg once daily.

items.t: Heart failure with renal impairment: no pharmacokinetic data; uptitrate with additional caution.

src.q: Uptitration of the dose in these populations should therefore be made with additional caution.

items.t: Severe liver impairment: no dose adjustment needed, but careful monitoring advised.

src.q: Patients with severe liver impairment No dosage adjustment is required, however careful monitoring is advised.

items.t: Heart failure with hepatic impairment: uptitrate with additional caution.

src.q: Uptitration of the dose in these populations should therefore be made with additional caution.

items.t: SmPC: should not be used in pregnancy unless clearly necessary. If used, monitor uteroplacental blood flow and fetal growth; monitor the newborn closely (hypoglycaemia, bradycardia, usually within 3 days).

src.q: Bisoprolol should not be used during pregnancy unless clearly necessary.
If treatment with bisoprolol is considered necessary, the uteroplacental blood flow and the fetal growth should be monitored.
Symptoms of hypoglycaemia and bradycardia are generally to be expected within the first 3 days.

items.t: BUMPS: can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; no concern about miscarriage or birth defects in the small number studied; extra growth scans may be offered.

src.q: Bisoprolol can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.
A small number of pregnant women taking bisoprolol have been studied, with no concerns raised that its use causes miscarriage or birth defects.
you may be offered additional scans at around 32 and 36 weeks

items.t: SmPC: not known whether excreted in milk; breastfeeding is not recommended.

src.q: breastfeeding is not recommended during administration of bisoprolol.

items.t: SPS: can be used with caution; labetalol, metoprolol or propranolol are preferred. Monitor the infant for bradycardia or hypoglycaemia.

src.q: Bisoprolol can be used with caution during breastfeeding, but labetalol, metoprolol, or propranolol are preferred if clinically appropriate.

reproductive.note: UK bisoprolol 5 mg SmPC: "Fertility No relevant data available." No contraception advice stated.

items.t: Common: dizziness, headache (mostly early, mild, settle in 1-2 weeks), cold or numb extremities, hypotension (especially heart failure), nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation, fatigue. Heart failure patients: very common bradycardia; common worsening heart failure and asthenia.

src.q: Common: dizziness*, headache*
Common: feeling of coldness or numbness in the extremities, hypotension especially in patient with heart failure.
Common: gastrointestinal complaints such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation.
Very common: bradycardia (in patients with chronic heart failure).
Common: worsening of pre-existing heart failure (in patients with chronic heart failure).

items.t: Uncommon: bronchospasm in asthma/obstructive airways disease, AV conduction disturbances. Rare: hepatitis, syncope, hypersensitivity incl. angioedema. Beta-blockers may provoke or worsen psoriasis.

src.q: Uncommon: bronchospasm in patients with bronchial asthma or a history of obstructive airways disease.
Rare: hepatitis.
Rare: hypersensitivity reactions (such as itching, flush, rash and angioedema).
Beta-blockers may provoke or worsen psoriasis or induce psoriasis-like rash, alopecia.

items.t: Overdose: bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, acute cardiac insufficiency, hypoglycaemia; heart failure patients are probably very sensitive.

src.q: The most common signs expected with overdose of a beta-blocker are bradycardia, hypotension, bronchospasm, acute cardiac insufficiency and hypoglycaemia.
patients with heart failure are probably very sensitive.
